prompt: A charting library has classes `BarSvg`, `BarPng`, `LineSvg`, `LinePng`, `PieSvg` and `PiePng`. Each pair duplicates its chart's layout code and differs only in how lines and shapes are drawn. A ticket asks for PDF output. What does this design predict, and what is the best change?

options.text: PDF needs one new class, `PdfChart`, because the chart types are already written
options.explanation: In this design, output format is baked into each chart class. PDF output needs a new class for every chart type, each copying that chart's layout code again.

options.text: Add a `Chart` base class with format-specific abstract methods, keeping one subclass per pair
options.explanation: A shared base class can remove some duplication, but it still leaves one class per chart-and-format pair. The two dimensions are still multiplied together.

options.text: Use an abstract factory that creates matching chart and renderer families
options.explanation: Abstract factory keeps families of products consistent. Here the problem is two independent dimensions multiplied into one hierarchy, not mixing mismatched parts.

options.text: PDF would need a class per chart type; split charts and renderers into two hierarchies and give each chart a renderer (a bridge), so PDF becomes one renderer class
options.explanation: Correct. Chart type and output format vary independently. A chart that holds a renderer lets each chart and each format be written once, so a new format is one class, provided every chart can be drawn through the same renderer interface.

workedExample:
1. Spot the two dimensions in the class names: chart type (bar, line, pie) and output format (SVG, PNG).
2. Predict the cost of the ticket: PDF needs `BarPdf`, `LinePdf` and `PiePdf`, each repeating its chart's layout. Every later chart type would also need one class per format.
3. Separate the dimensions:

```
Chart --has a--> Renderer
Bar, Line, Pie   Svg, Png, Pdf
```

4. Now the layout code lives once per chart, and drawing code lives once per format. PDF is one new `Pdf` renderer.
5. Check the assumption before refactoring: the bridge only pays off if every chart can draw itself through the same small renderer interface (lines, shapes, text). If PDF needed special code for each chart type, part of the duplication would return.
